title: Falo, falas, fala — regular -ar verbs
goal: Master the biggest verb pattern in Portuguese — verbs ending in *-ar* — then use it to ask questions and say no. This is the third hurdle, and the price you pay for being allowed to drop your pronouns.
bekal: produce the five present-tense forms of *-ar* verbs without looking at the table
ask questions three ways, including the typically Portuguese *é que*
make sentences negative with *não* — and know why *não* often appears twice

dialogs.title: Diálogo — Duas rotinas
dialogs.intro: Ana and Budi sit down at a coffee shop that's finally open. They start asking each other about their daily lives.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.literal: where is it that you-live, Budi?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Moro em Alfama, num quarto pequeno.
lines.id: I live in Alfama, in a small room.
lines.literal: I-live in Alfama, in-a room small.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.id: And do you work here in Lisbon?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Não, não trabalho. Estudo português numa escola.
lines.id: No, I don't work. I study Portuguese at a school.
lines.literal: no, not I-work. I-study Portuguese in-a school.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: A que horas é que começam as aulas?
lines.id: What time do the classes start?
lines.literal: at what hours is it that they-start the(pl) classes?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Começam às nove. Estudamos quatro horas por dia.
lines.id: They start at nine. We study four hours a day.
lines.literal: they-start at-the(pl) nine. we-study four hours per day.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.id: And do you talk with Portuguese people?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Falo com a dona Fernanda. Ela fala devagar.
lines.id: I talk with Dona Fernanda. She speaks slowly.
lines.literal: I-speak with the lady Fernanda. she she-speaks slowly.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Ah, os meus amigos falam muito depressa!
lines.id: Oh, my friends speak really fast!
lines.literal: ah, the(pl) my(pl) friends they-speak very fast!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Pois. E não pronunciam as vogais!
lines.id: Exactly. And they don't pronounce the vowels!
lines.literal: indeed. and not they-pronounce the(pl) vowels!

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Pois é. Mas tu escutas bem.
lines.id: That's how it is. But you have good ears.
lines.literal: indeed is. but you you-listen well.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I listen, but I don't always understand!

notes: **Onde é que moras?** — a construction you'll hear hundreds of times in Portugal. Literally it means "where is it that you live", and in meaning it's exactly the same as *Onde moras?*. The extra *é que* changes nothing except making the sentence sound more natural and easier to say. Use it — it saves you from having to flip the word order.

**Não trabalho, with não before the verb.** There's no helper word like English *don't*. Just put *não* right before the verb, and you're done. When answering a question, *não* often appears twice: the first answers "no", the second negates the sentence — *Não, não trabalho.*
**Num, numa** — *em* fused with *um* and *uma*: *num quarto*, *numa escola*. Just like *no* and *na*, which you saw in Unit 2. These contractions are never split.

**Cá** means "here", just like *aqui* — but it feels warmer and more Portuguese. People say *anda cá* ("come here"), *cá em casa* ("here at our place"). *Aqui* is always correct; *cá* makes you sound like you've lived there for a while.

**Pois** and **pois é** are the two most Portuguese words there are. *Pois* agrees with something just said ("exactly", "right"), and *pois é* acknowledges a slightly unwelcome fact ("that's how it is"). Neither has a neat English equivalent, and both belong in your vocabulary.
**Nem sempre** = "not always". *Nem* is a combined "and not / not even", and it shows up in many constructions: *nem eu* (me neither), *nem sequer* (not even).

grammars.title: Verbs ending in -ar in the present
body: This is the biggest group: roughly **three out of four** Portuguese verbs end in *-ar*, and almost all of them follow this pattern with no surprises. Drop the *-ar* from the infinitive, then add these five endings.
after: **Listen closely to the difference between *fala* and *falam*.** The first ends in a plain *a*, the second in a **nasal** one — and that's the only thing separating "he speaks" from "they speak". In fast speech the difference is very slight. When you're not sure, context comes to the rescue.
The *nós* form (*falamos*) happens to be identical to its past-tense form, which you'll learn in Unit 14. That's not a problem — the Portuguese rely on context to tell them apart too.
**The pronoun is dropped, except for emphasis.** *Falo português* is complete. *Eu falo português, ela fala inglês* uses the pronouns because two people are being compared.

grammars.title: Three ways to ask a question
body: Portuguese has no question helper like English *do*. Making a question is much cheaper.

head: Method
Form
Example
rows: *Onde é que moras?* — **the most common in Portugal**
*Onde moras tu?* — correct, but sounds more written

after: Question words to learn now: *o que* (what), *quem* (who), *onde* (where), *quando* (when), *como* (how), *porque* (why), *quanto* (how much), *qual* (which).

**Watch the pair *porquê* and *porque*.** To ask, write *Porque é que...?* or *Porquê?* on its own. To answer, write *porque* ("because") — and the answer needs no special order: *Porque é que estudas português? — Porque gosto da língua.*
The question word *o que* almost always comes with *é que* in conversation: *O que é que fazes?* In fast speech it gets squeezed until it sounds like "kuh-kuh FAH-zuhsh".

grammars.title: Saying no
body: One word is enough, and it always goes in the same place: **right before the verb.**
after: **Double negatives are right, not wrong.** *Não falo nada* = "I don't say anything" (literally "I don't say nothing"). *Não vejo ninguém* = "I don't see anyone" (literally "I don't see nobody"). In standard English this counts as a mistake; in Portuguese it's **obligatory**.
If *nunca*, *ninguém* or *nada* comes **before** the verb, *não* is dropped: *Nunca falo com eles* — not *não nunca*.

blocks.text: Every verb below follows the *falar* pattern with no exceptions. Once you know those five endings, you've mastered this whole list.

blocks.title: Two verbs that always bring de
items: *gostar* and *precisar* never stand alone — both must be followed by **de**: *gosto **de** café*, *preciso **de** ajuda*. When the noun has an article, *de* fuses with it: *gosto **do** café*, *preciso **da** chave*.

This is one of the most stubborn mistakes for English speakers, because "like" and "need" take a direct object with no preposition. *Gosto café* is always wrong. Practice by saying *gostar de* as one single word.
*gostar* is fully covered in Unit 11, along with how to give your opinion.

blocks.text: Their position is flexible, but the safest place is **after the verb**: *Falo sempre português em casa.* The word *nunca* is an exception that prefers to stand **in front**: *Nunca falo inglês aqui.*
The pair *já* and *ainda não* is used constantly for short answers. *Já almoçaste? — Ainda não.* ("Have you had lunch? — Not yet.") Notice that the answer doesn't repeat the verb at all.
